en.justification: Pilgrimages to Our Lady of the Snow were widespread, especially in Croatia. The cult comes from Rome and is related to the oldest cult of the Virgin Mary known in the Esquiline Hills.
The Virgin Mary is shown as the protector of people of all social ranks – peasants, priests and the nobility.
The homily was an important part of the pilgrim mass.
The votive sculpture is accompanied by saints as both protectors and helpers.
The entrance to the high altar, accompanied by two side-altars, shows scenes from the history of the place as a site of pilgrimage dedicated to the pain of the Virgin Mary.
The main painting of the church explains the divine plan of Salvation as told in both the Old and New Testaments of the Bible.
The three-part altar represents the Holy Cross pilgrimage shrine.
Even among Roman Legionnaires, allegedly, pictures of the Virgin Mary were revered. The pilgrimage to the "Mary of the four pillars" is first described in the 13th century.

One of the most used scenes in the iconography around the Virgin Mary. According to dogma, the Virgin Mary "having completed the course of her earthly life”, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. The feast day of Assumption in August is the biggest feast day of the Christian calendar.

en.location: Wilten Basilica
en.justification: Like the rhetoric of a preacher, the content of Late Baroque imagery brought to the fore many references. Here is Judith who presented the head of Holofernes as a symbol of triumph over evil. The image would have been interpreted by people as a precursor of the Virgin Mary; Judith, who at the end of all time was the "apocalyptic woman" and the conqueror of all evil.

The first chapel, devoted to St. Rupert, was built during the lifetime of St. Notburga (c. 1313). The cult of St. Notburga grew up after 1430; she was an Austrian saint from modern-day Tyrol and the patron saint of servants and peasants.

en.location: Catholic Parish and Pilgrimage Church of St. Notburga
en.justification: Exhumation of the corpse of St. Notburga preceded reconstruction of the Baroque church. The bones of the saints were then honoured as integrated whole-body relics in rich robes within a glass case on the high altar.

en.location: Catholic Parish and Pilgrimage Church of St. Notburga
en.justification: The massive two-storey free-standing altar with pillars and a canopy in the extract, acts as a sort of triumphal gateway between earth and heaven, with the saints as mediators.

en.location: Catholic Parish and Pilgrimage Church of St. Notburga
en.artist: Fresco: Johann Georg Höttinger oder Christoph Anton Mayr; stuccowork: Franz Xaver Feichtmayr
en.justification: The paintings on the ceiling present scenes from the life of the saint.
The wide horizontal façade invites pilgrims to come in.

The origin of the sanctuary is linked to a legend, according to which, a figure of Our Lord was thrown into the water by Nicodemos in Palestine and later reached Matosinhos on 3 May 124 (AD). On its journey, however, the figure had lost an arm, which no artist was able to replicate. Allegedly, sometime later, an old woman was surprised by a dry branch that kept springing out from the fire, and she eventually recognised it as the missing arm from the figure.
In the centre of the altar stands the miraculous image of Our Lord of Matosinhos flanked by Late Renaissance stone figures.
The side-chapels complete the Holy space of the pilgrimage church.
A typical Croatian pilgrimage church surrounded by vaulted arcades and furnished with altars, some of which are of exceptional quality, painted by the Slovenian painter A. J. Lerchinger.

The legend of a Franciscan lay-brother who found a small statue of the Virgin Mary under some ruins in Jerusalem is the central subject of the ceiling painting on the apse vault, surrounded by four medallions depicting scenes from the Life of the Virgin Mary: *Birth of the Virgin Mary*, the *Visitation*, the *Annunciation*, and the *Immaculate Conception*.
The much-admired sculpture of the Virgin Mary on the main altar.
A place for spiritual meditation on the mystery of death and resurrection, the partly-constructed rooms are completely covered with skulls and bones.
The church is devoted to the Holy Cross, a symbol of resurrection.
The crypt contains the mummified bodies of mostly monks as well as the architects of the monastery.
Baron Trenck was a famous soldier who was born in Calabria and died in Brno. He spent his entire inheritance on building the Capuchin Monastery.

St. Helen is believed to embody a portrait of Empress Eleonora, in whose honour the picture was painted. The painting was said to have been commissioned by the Count of Lobkowitz, one of the most powerful men of the Viennese imperial court.
Count Rottal added a memorial chapel and family tomb to the parish church of his residence.

en.detail_name: Christ on the mount of Olives
en.justification: The scene shows the process of death which is made all the more impactful by the symbolic black and white combination.
Life-size portraits of the investor and his wife adorn the side altars, presenting them as art-loving and pious aristocrats.
Life-size portraits of the investor and his wife adorn the side altars, presenting them as art-loving and pious aristocrats.

The fortifications of a castle were part of the reconstruction concept conceived to glorify an ancient dynasty by means of a “*via triumphalis*”, the main feature of which is the unique Hall of the Ancestors perched upon the promontory.
The memorial building celebrates a Swabian-Bavarian dynasty that settled in Moravia in the second-half of the 16th century. There is also a mausoleum.
The family’s celestial triumph is accompanied by scenes depicting aristocratic virtues.
Niche statues represent real and mythical family figures.

The founder of the dynasty, Palatin Pál, built a family mausoleum in the Franciscan Church in Kismarton (Eisenstadt), within the residential area that formed part of his large estates. The design of the sepulchral chapel, which was determined by the Cult of the Virgin Mary, represents the material element of Prince Pál’s patronage.

Members of the Esterházy family are kneeling in the niches of the chapel in gestures of eternal worship. They are turned toward the Virgin Mary who is mourning her son, which suggests that they have committed themselves to her patronage, not only in life, but also in death.
The concept of the tomb included funerary symbolism and associated allegories of life, death, resurrection and celestial afterlife.

An example of a parish church that also functioned as a pilgrimage church to the cultic image of St. Mary’s Aid (Cult of the Virgin Mary). This was the prototype for most late Tyrolean parish churches.

en.name: High altar and image
en.justification: The high altar presents the famous cultic image of St. Mary’s Aid. This was the prototype for a host of copies that spread throughout Central Europe.

en.name: Tomb of archduke Maximilian III
en.justification: Most parish churches are also places of burial.
An example of a so-called peasant’s cathedral; a monumental double-towered church with a richly decorated interior.
The imposing interior in the Louis-XVI style is quite the opposite of the simple exterior.

The church was commissioned by a countess on the foundations of another Gothic building. With the help of donations from the under-governor, it was given the Baroque treatment with the addition of chapels and a covered walkway.
Various votive pieces, mostly paintings and small gifts (models of healed body parts) were placed in the walkway.
While the local community financed the pulpit, members of the aristocracy were among the donors for the rest of the furnishings.
A small church donated by citizens during a plague epidemic in the 1630s.
Urban parish church with a tripartite group of altars and several annexed chapels dedicated to local cults.

Private ceremonies, including baptism, confirmation, marriage and funerals took place at the parish church. Festivities relating to various religious feasts were also celebrated (i.e. Easter, Corpus Christi, Assumption, and All Saints).

The most characteristic feature of the North Croatian Baroque landscape is its wooden churches. The many images of different saints in these simple buildings are typical devotional objects. associated with peasants.
The bearded St. Kümerrnissa was particularly popular in Tyrol and can be traced back to the Middle Ages. Her unusual looks relate to the *Volto Santo* (Holy Face) from the Tuscan city of Lucca.

The image within, praised by angels, is a reproduction of a painting of the adoration of the Virgin Mary of Znojmo which originated in the 1630s. The subject of the de Herdt painting is the miraculous transport of the original painting, which, according to legend, was brought to its new location by angels.

The coronation of the miraculous picture of the Virgin Mary in Brno was one of the largest religious celebrations to take place on Czech territory. To mark the occasion, the Augustinians ordered a retable and liturgical set from a famous workshop in Augsburg.
The palladium of Moravia, a miraculous picture of the Madonna and Child, was donated to the Augustinian monastery in Brno by Emperor Charles IV.

The radial monstrance is decorated with vine leaves, grapes and the Eucharist, the symbol of Christ’s blood. Below the casket in relief are the Madonna and Child; at the top, under a baldachin, is God and the dove of the Holy Spirit. Cartouches on the richly wrought pedestal feature Madonna of Old Brno and half-figures of saints of the order painted on enamel.

The spiral part of the sceptre is covered with acanthus leaves and multi-coloured cut-glass. In the central halo there is an image of the Madonna of Old Brno transferred into relief form as a cast statue.

Celebrations for the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns of the Moravian margraviate. The Holy Virgin became queen and patron saint of Moravia. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with pyrotechnical effects.

This is a popular type of Immaculate Virgin that evolved during the Catholic revival, where the Virgin is at prayer on top of a globe and a crescent moon and stands on the head of a serpent which symbolises evil.
The uniquely shaped monstrance encompassing the Immaculate Virgin Mary was created as a part of the decoration of the Pilgrim Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná.
During the Baroque period, monstrances became decorative objects intended for adoration while also retaining the practical function of carrying the Holy Communion.
This votive-type of Virgin and Child first appeared during the Baroque period. The cult of the Blessed Virgin Mary was central to the iconography of the period.
First a new altar was built in honour of the miraculous picture of the Virgin Mary; some years later the church was enlarged to accommodate the many visitors that came to see the image.

Construction of the long, sinuous portico began as a result of contributions from religious orders, noble families, guilds and private citizens all of whom wanted to admire the miraculous picture of the Virgin Mary.
The internal space of the church is defined by the adoption of half- and free-standing columns, which convey the impression of a cross-shaped plan.
The theatrical gate of the pilgrim complex amplifies its significance as a mystic place of local worship.
A most important and popular place of pilgrimage that was founded, according to the legend, as a result of two elderly people who dreamt about Our Lady.
These 18th-century panels recall the legend of the miraculous finding of the image of Our Lady on the site.
The main altarpiece includes a reliquary in gilt silver. Donated by pilgrims, it holds the image of Our Lady of Cape Espichel.
The interior of the water house has running benches and is decorated with scenes of leisure and pilgrimage.

Legend has it that saints Cyril and Methodius once baptised pagans in Křtiny Valley. The architect, Santini, was acquainted with the numerical symbolism of the Jewish Cabbala, also developed by prominent Catholic scholars, and applied its principles to this extraordinary composition.

The statue dates from the first-half of the 14th century. The significance of the pilgrimage site grew during the Thirty Years’ War, when it became a destination for two major thanksgiving pilgrimages to the Virgin Mary, who was protectoress of the country.
The ceiling painting is a metaphorical celebration of the Virgin Mary as the embodiment of Divine Wisdom. Angels with mirrors serve to enlighten visitors.
The model shows the ideal appearance of the church and residence which were never completed. The ground-plan symbolises the Marian star.

This extraordinary pilgrimage complex was built as a site of mediation for Christ’s suffering and death. The location of the site evokes Golgotha, with the church as a metaphorical representation of the Temple of Jerusalem.

A striking semi-folk interior enhances the mystical air of the church, which was among about 140 sites in rural areas in the region where the pilgrimage tradition was particularly strong, and where hosts of pilgrims would gather in order to “find the wellspring of all virtue”.

The convex–concave frontage traces the ground-plan. The blind central entrance is particularly remarkable and probably symbolically embodies the third gate of St. John’s Revelation. Stone coats-of-arms of the founder of the church and his wife appear above the staircase, while a central cartouche features the bull of Pope Clement XI. Ledges that sit above crosses in shallow niches may symbolise the crown of thorns worn by Christ.

The high altar includes a replica picture of the Saviour (*Salvatore*) given blessing in Laterano, near Rome, where the original is to be found. In front of the high altar, two tombstones cover the entrance to an underground crypt of the founder.
Symbolic church building in a cruciform shape.

The veneration of St. Cross of Pill is due to an event involving Bavarian troops in Tyrol during the War of Spanish Succession. Allegedly, during a battle, a bridge burned down and a cross from it fell into the river below Pill, from where it was rescued unharmed. Soon after, the cross was considered miraculous.
A miraculous 17th-century crucifix adorns the main altar.
An Early Baroque example of church architecture symbolic of pilgrimage: the rotunda form alludes to the Pantheon, the old Marianic Sanctuary of Rome.

en.name: Main altar
en.location: Pilgrimage Church of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows
en.artist: Design: Konstantin Pader; altarpiece: Johann Hehrl
en.justification: The interior has a double-sided liturgical system: opposite the main altar, special triumphal architecture is located in veneration of the former pear tree, which had once contained the cultic image.

en.name: Main altar
en.location: Pilgrimage Church of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows
en.artist: Design: Konstantin Pader; altarpiece: Johann Hehrl
en.justification: The miraculous image was found in a pear tree on land where a church was later built.

The monastery on the hill at Rijeka, which dates back to the 13th century, was founded in veneration of the legend of the transportation of the Holy House of Loreto from the Holy Land to Trsat in Rijeka. According to the legend, angels brought the Holy House to the Franciscan church and dedicated it to the Virgin Mary.
The side-altar was donated by the Rovere family, who are depicted together with their saint-protectors.
The altar devoted to “St Anne selfthird” (St. Anne with others) is an eternal remembrance of the Rovere family who lived in 17th century.
Detail of the Rovere children.

The triumphal composition of the painting on the high-altar presents the patron saint of Hungary. Painted in the last years of the so-called Balkan Campaign, it illustrated for the faithful their release from Turkish rule.

The painting was commissioned by the Government of Bologna to thank the Virgin of the Rosary after the end of the plague in 1630. Originally it was used as a standard and carried in an annual procession to commemorate the end of the epidemic.
The painting was commisioned by a burgher of Tata for the Piarists in whose school his son was probably educated. In the main, this picture refers to the educational activities of the Piarist order.

The picture is a typical example of a votive painting designed for a town environment. In their everyday prayers and pledges, people of the town turned to saints as protectors against the various perils of life.
The painter, Johann Jakob Zeiller, decorated his own home with sacred and allegorical frescoes that are framed within the cult of the Virgin Mary.

en.detail_name: Detail with image of St. Mary´s Aid
en.justification: The cult of the Virgin Mary is seen in the image of St. Mary’s Aid which is common throughout Tyrol and Bavaria. Placed on the façade, the image functions as a protective symbol.
The Jesuit Chapel, novitiate of St. Ignatius, was created for private worship, especially for the prayers of novices.
The glory of the saint being escorted to heaven by angels is clearly self-celebratory, alluding to the powerful religious order that was founded by him.
The Jesuits not only played a central role in the restoration of Győr’s infrastructure after the Tukish occupation, but also nurtured the spiritual, cultural and educational life of the town too.

The construction and interior decoration of the church was largely financed by patrons among whom were the Archbishop and Bishop of Győr, other members of the chapter and the families of children who attended the Jesuit school.

Beside traditional Jesuit iconography, specific features of Hungarian iconography from the period are also evident, such as those relating to the Ottoman wars and the closely related theme of the *Regnum Marianum/Patrona Hungariae* (St. Stephen offering the country to the Virgin Mary). All the saints, kings and bishops lined up in the decorative programme were founders and supporters of the Catholic Hungarian Kingdom and defenders against the infidels or non-believers (images of Turks and Protestants appear on the altars).

After the plague of 1630, the Madonna of the Rosary became the centre of a new religious zeal. Many of the people who had survived the epidemic arrived at the chapel bearing votive gifts in thanks for their survival.

This pilgrimage church is one of the most remarkable buildings in Europe. The building visually mythologises a previously insignificant place and presents its origin as a divine miracle. Here, a learned abbot of the Cistercian monastery established a “spiritual mausoleum” for John of Nepomuk, a saint canonised in 1729, whose cult became one of the most widespread in Central Europe.

The establishment of the church was associated with the upcoming beatification and canonisation of John of Nepomuk, following the miraculous discovery of the saint’s intact tongue at his grave in St. Vitus Cathedral, Prague. The construction was initiated by the abbot of the nearby Cistercian Monastery in Žďár, who named the hill above it after Zelená Hora near Nepomuk, the martyr’s birthplace, and the place from which the first Cistercians left to come to Žďár.
The church is surrounded by a cemetery. Branching off the walkway are chapels where prayers are said and votive gifts are placed.
The whole building is permeated with symbols of the saint.

Although the nearby market town had been legally protected against raids in the Thirty Years’ War, the wealthy citizens who lived there promised to donate votive gifts of thanks and in honour of St. Anthony.
The church is located above the village on the slope of a mountain. It served local inhabitants as well as pilgrims and merchants travelling on the Alpine transit routes.

The pilgrimage church was part of a large residential network attached to a major Premonstratensian monastery in Znojmo-Louka. The monastery hospital, for former members of the order, was close to the church where the miraculous healing sculpture of the Saviour was kept.

The miraculous statue was brought by a monk of the Premonstratensian order from the Steingaden Monastery in Bavaria. It is a replica of an adoration statue in the local Wieskirche. The statue was first placed on a side altar in the old Church of St. Lawrence, but as it was believed to heal the sick and as such enjoyed enormous respect, a new church was built on the site, and the statue was installed on the high altar.
The sophisticated iconography is typical of monastery pilgrimage churches.
The decoration was determined by the church’s dedication to the Scourged Christ, one of only a few church’s worldwide dedicated to this aspect of the Passion.
Lacquered *namban* oratory with floral designs in *maki-e* (sprinkled gold and silver powder) and *raden* (mother-of-pearl inlay) with a painting of the Virgin Mary with the infant Jesus in her arms.
Lacquered *namban* oratory with floral designs in *maki-e* (sprinkled gold and silver powder) and *raden* (mother-of-pearl inlay) with a painting of the Virgin Mary with the infant Jesus in her arms.
A so-called sun monstrance from Zagreb Cathedral illustrating the Passion of Christ. It is covered with filigree work, a series of bands with foliate ornamentation, jewels and enamel medallions.

The lifeless body of Christ creates deep and intense psychological tension to visually impart the values inherited from the Council of Trent. The dual rhetoric of *docere* and *delectare* (to teach, to move and to delight) in this context, suggests that man is elevated to eternity through the inner drama of the Passion.
The sculpture is based on a composition by Rubens.

The sculpted images of great dimensions are based on models that circulated throughout Europe within the context of depictions of the death and Crucifixion of Christ. The theme exemplifies one that was widespread in Portuguese art from the 16th through to the 17th century, in response to the most essential ideals of the Council of Trent.

The Catholic devotion to the Blessed Sacrament, reinforced by the Counter-Reformation, developed into a type of monumental monstrance that played a key role within the adoration of the *Corpus Christi* or Blessed Sacrament.

en.name: *Our Lady of Rosary*
en.location: Chiesa della Natività di Maria, Portoferraio, Isola d'Elba, Italy
en.justification: Victory at the Battle of Lepanto was attributed to the Blessed Virgin Mary after a rosary procession was offered on that day, in St. Peter’s Square in Rome, for the success of the mission of the Holy League to hold back Muslim forces from overrunning Western Europe.

en.name: Goblet
en.location: Portoferraio, Isola d'Elba, Italy

en.justification: A famous site of pilgrimage in southern Bavaria and of great importance in Central Europe. Pilgrimage, the monastery’s activities and its connections all make this an important meeting point for people of all social classes.
Copies of this miraculous statue gave rise to several pilgrimage sites in central Europe, such as in Dyje.

en.name: The Last Judgement
en.location: Pilgrimage Church of the Scourged Saviour
en.justification: The ceiling-painting depicts the promise of healing and the Last Judgment as the target of the redemptive work of Christ, which began with His suffering before the Crucifixion. Opposite the gate to eternity, before which Cronus was overthrown (symbolic of the end of time), Christ prepares the Judge's throne.

en.name: Presbyterium with the main altar
en.location: Pilgrimage Church of the Scourged Saviour
en.artist: Architect for the altar: Dominikus Zimmermann (1685–1766); sculptures: Ägid Verhelst (1696–1749); altarpiece: Balthasar Augustin Albrecht (1687–1765)
en.justification: Construction of the church came about as a result of a miracle involving a miraculous weeping statue. This gave rise to the Procession of the Scourged Saviour, which processed to the church on the meadow where the figure had been rediscovered.
The oratory was built by the Brotherhood of the Holy Trinity, whose task it was to provide assistance to poor pilgrims and convalescent facilities to patients from a nearby hospital.
The first story in the cycle represents the creation of man, seen as the greatest gesture of God’s love for mankind.

The church and cloister of the Order of St. Basil in the Munkács (Mukachevo, Ukraine) Eparchy, was an important centre of the Greek Catholic Church in historical Hungary. It was where the Western and Eastern Churches of Byzantine ritual met before they joined with Rome in 1646.

en.name: Weeping Mary from Máriapócs
en.location:
Altar of the Virgin Mary, Church of Worship and Basilian Monastery of Máriapócs  
Máriapócs, Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg county
en.justification: The original was commissioned as a votive painting in gratitude for his release from Turkish captivity. Following the first act of weeping, Emperor Leopold I had the painting transferred to Vienna, where it was finally placed in St. Stephen’s Dome on the day that the troops of Prince Eugene of Savoy defeated the Turkish armies. The people of Vienna related the triumph to the miraculous power of the “Mary of Pócs”, which the emperor confirmed.
Located on top of a hill, this place of pilgrimage is an example of the spread of *sacromonte* (sacred hill).
The pilgrimage site comprises a church and an enormous stairway that begins in the Garden of the Kings decorated with a central fountain.

Water is an important element at places of pilgrimage, signifying the separation of water and earth when God created the World. Water is also a symbol of purification in both the spiritual and physical senses of the word.
The interior of the church is decorated with three carved, gilt-wood altarpieces.

Construction of the church was inspired by the miraculous recovery of a local miller’s daughter after praying to the statue of the Virgin Mary, and is said to have been brought from the Minorite Monastery in Brno.
The church, where the founder is also buried, was built next to what had once been a homestead, but which is now the parsonage.

en.name: Virgin Mary of Dolours
en.location:
Pilgrimage Church of the Virgin Mary of Dolours  
Sloup, Moravia
en.artist:
Sculpture: Italian artist?  
Main altar: Ondřej Schweigl (1735–1812, Brno)
en.justification: To this day, people come from neighbouring countries to admire the miraculous sculpture.

The central scene of the ceiling painting, placed in an illusory architectural frame, is supplemented by allegories of the Virtues. The lower section features angels who are spreading pilgrimage devotionalia from a cornucopia.
The figure might be St. Hieronymus, one of the Church Fathers. The pedestal shows that the object was a reliquary. The Bust is one in a series of original decorations of altar tables in a church.
Processional standard of the Brotherhood of the Tears of the Virgin Mary or of the Ponte del Borgo, later known as the Company of the Holy Sacrament.

A silver processional altar which once belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi-Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies.
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist.
Reliquary shaped as a portrait bust devoted to St. Stephan the King, which was donated to Zagreb Cathedral Treasury by Francesco Barberini, a member of the powerful Italian family.
Chest with engraved low-relief featuring scenes from life in the service of the mission and martyrdom. Commissioned by King Pedro II of Portugal, it paid royal homage to the Jesuit saint.
The vestment is clearly indebted to models made in Rome during the papacy of Benedict XIV and is similar to those donated to St. Peter’s Cathedral.
The large stairway endowed with chapels, statues and allegorical fountains leading up to the pilgrimage sanctuary represents the typology of the *Sacro Monte*.

en.location: The Stairway of the Five Senses, Bom Jesus de Braga Sanctuary (Bom Jesus do Monte)
en.justification: The stairway of the Five Senses leads up to the Crucifixion Chapel. The way up is punctuated by other chapels, such as the Chapel of the Flagellation, which reinforces the *Via Crucis* (Christ’s Sufferening) as an element of purification.

en.location: The Stairway of the Five Senses, Bom Jesus de Braga Sanctuary (Bom Jesus do Monte)
en.justification: The motto for the theme of the Senses is introduced at the first fountain referring precisely to the Suffering of Christ and presenting the symbolism that summarises the *Via Crucis*. The instruments of Christ’s Passion are presented on the fountain-tablet in relief.

en.location: Bom Jesus Church, Bom Jesus de Braga Sanctuary (Bom Jesus do Monte)
en.justification: A monumental representation of Calvary with life-size figures furnishes the main altar of the church, which is located on top of a hill.
With a spatially segmented frontage opening onto the countryside, the pilgrimage complex is a typical example of Counter-Reformation architecture.

en.detail_name: *Vision of the Virgin Mary by a Olomouc burgher*
en.justification: Legend has it that the chapel was built on the hill by an Olomouc burgher after he had a vision of the Virgin Mary while at the site.
The church was granted the status of “basilica minor”, which meant that pilgrims could receive the same indulgences there as they could at Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome.
Through the interplay of light and colour and the transition of the altar architecture into the stucco decoration of the vault, the baldachin accentuates the centrepiece of this pilgrimage complex.

The bridge was a fixed route for pilgrims heading for Saint Peter’s tomb. St Peter was the first bishop of the Christian church and was buried in St. Peter’s Cathedral in the Vatican in Rome. The angels, holding symbols of the Sorrows of the Christ, encourage penitence.

The devotional column and chapel celebrate the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. It was built on the initiative of a local master-stonemason who oversaw the construction and also contributed the preliminary finance.
The sculpture at the top of the column is Christ the Saviour and God the Father, the ruler of the world, which opens out to the Archangel Michael, the symbol of the eternal struggle with heresy.
The column presents the largest grouping of Baroque statues within a single sculpture in Central Europe. The six statues on the central section represent Slavic saints.

Light played a major role in Baroque iconography, because as a symbol of the Holy Spirit it was seen as synonymous with holiness. Angels, the mediators of God's will, are represented in the bottom balustrade of the staircase as decorative *putti*, seen as both messengers and guardians of the light.
An example of a recently canonised saint who is celebrated by a church dedicated to him. The church was built close to the summer palace of the Pope.
Pairs of angels on the window-displays hold up eight medallions illustrating miraculous episodes of St. Thomas of Villanova.

en.name: Glory of St. Thomas
en.location: Side altar, St. Thomas of Villanova church, Castel Gandolfo
en.justification: Pope Alexander VII decided to dedicate the church to the new saint as a symbol of active charity.

The bridge, located on a major communication route, connects a chateau and the area below it with the town, church and monastery. Statues of saints are lined up on the bridge, the objective being that “even strangers passing by may worship God in public through His saints, to the disgrace of heretics”.
The two angels that guard the entrace to the bridge personify the guardian spirits believed to accompany pilgrims and travellers.
Saints were selected on the basis of the personal piousness of the investors and their families.

St. John of Nepomuk was a popular saint frequently considered the protector of roads, but also of bridges, because a bridge marked the manner of his death: he was thrown in the Vltava from Charles Bridge in 1393.

This iconographically interesting altarpiece was commissioned by the noble Ratta family. The two saints either side of the Virgin Mary are Petronius, Bishop and patron of Bologna, and Dionysius, martyr and bishop of Paris, who is often mixed-up with the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th- to early 6th century. Saint Dionysius was probably painted on request of the patrons, as one of the members of the Ratta family was a diplomat sent by the Pope to France in order to persuade Louis XIV to abolish the Edict of Nantes and resume persecution of the Huguenots.

en.name: Bust of St. Barbara
en.location: Church of St. James, Porto Azzurro, Isola d'Elba, Italy
en.justification: The half-figure of the popular saint shows a strong expression of the belief in eternity.

For this commission, Algardi carefully studied the death-mask of the saint, who died in 1595 and was sanctified in 1622. The saint’s face, which shows the strain of old age and suffering, also reflects his deep humanity, humility and the extraordinary strength of one so close to God.

en.location: Basilica, Galilee, National Palace of Mafra
en.justification: The sculpture collection, which could be seen as a kind of mausoleum of saints, makes illusion to the notion of heaven on earth.

en.location: Basilica, Galilee, National Palace of Mafra
en.justification: Depicting the two martyrs St. Sebastian and St. Vincent, these sculptures are from the royal commission of 56 Italian sculptures, which is one of the most important collections of Italian Baroque sculpture outside Italy.

en.location: Basilica, Galilee, National Palace of Mafra
en.justification: Made from marble, each sculpture is 3.58-metres tall.

On the three inferior corners of the base are cherubs and three figures that symbolise Faith, Hope and Charity. On the superior corners are three full-length angels conveying motifs of the Eucharist, which intertwine with six cherubs and seraphs ascending along the stem.
On the three faces of the base, oval bas-reliefs represent themes from the Eucharist: The Supper at Emmaus and the giant bunch of grapes, Fruit from the Promised Land and Christ at Calvary.

Mögel’s paintings served the improvement of general taste while also evoking a pious disposition. The illusory painting, which creates a milieu for the depiction of the saints, also raises to the status of art the pious printed pictures that had been popular since the Middle Ages. At the same time, Mogel continues a century-long tradition of religious still-life painting.
